body:
Poet's Toolkit: "Thunder Visits": 1. Three stanzas, four lines each. 2. "like a giant in a hurry"; it compares thunder, loud and stomping, to a giant rushing down the hill. 3. Any two: "comes stomping down the hill" (stomping); "rattles every windowsill" (rattling); "grumbles, yawns, and sighs" (grumbling, yawning, sighing); "wanders off to bed" (going to bed). Also the clouds "pull on their coats," the wind "runs off to hide," the sun "peeks out with sleepy eyes." 4. gray/bay and hide/side; the first and third lines rhyme and the second and fourth lines rhyme (ABAB). 5. The sound of rain tapping fast and steady, like fingers drumming on a table. 6. It starts loud and noisy (stomping, rattles, shakes) and ends calm and sleepy (yawns, sighs, sleepy eyes).
Poem or Story? The Morning Bus: 1. The poem is in short lines, grouped into two stanzas, with a title; it does not use full sentences in every line. 2. The poem has a steady beat of about four strong beats, then three; the story has no regular beat. 3. cold/rolls (near rhyme), cloud/loud, aisle/mile, free/me; rhyme makes it musical and easy to remember. 4. Example: the bus doors: "the bus doors opened with a hiss" versus "a hiss, a sigh, out loud." Also the time, the cold, the breath, the window seat. 5. A metaphor; her breath in the cold air looks like a small cloud. 6. Either; the answer gives an example from the chosen version.
What the Poet Means: "Grandpa's Hands": The metaphor compares his hands to maps: the blue veins look like rivers and the wrinkles like roads, and like a map, the hands show everywhere they have been and everything they have done. Other examples: "slow as Sunday" (simile: slow and unhurried, like a quiet day off); "they dance across the boat" (personification: quick and graceful when fishing). Theme: a grandparent's hands carry a lifetime of work and love, and they will keep teaching the next generation; the map metaphor shows the past and the journey ahead.
Poetry Check: "The Old Oak in Winter": 1. Three stanzas of four lines; pairs of lines rhyme (AABB: field/shield, deep/asleep, sky/by, ice/twice, door/more, see/tree). 2. A metaphor; the oak is strong, tough and refuses to give in, and its bark protects it like a shield. 3. Stubborn means refusing to give up or change; "but the old oak never falls asleep" and "The wind pushes hard ... but" show it will not give in. 4. "Its branches are arms ... waving to geese" (waving), "It wears a white scarf of frost," or "the squirrels say thank you." 5. "like a friend at the door"; spring returning is compared to a friend coming back, because it is welcome and familiar. 6. Theme: being patient and strong helps you get through hard times; supported by "It has stood through a hundred winters" and "Being patient is part of being a tree."
Scoring tip: count "the oak never falls asleep" as personification too if the student explains it; a student who names the device but does not explain it is Developing on the figurative criterion.
title: Answer key: Poems and Figurative Language
